title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
content:
The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.
“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said “the exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”
An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.
It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.
The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.
Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.
The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.
Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms,” and that “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.
The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.
The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.
In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.
In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.
It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.
It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.

report.summary: The IMF warns that a crash in AI share prices, amplified by heavy borrowing and concentrated tech exposure, could threaten global financial stability.
report.background: The AI boom has driven US equity markets to record concentration, with the 'magnificent seven' tech giants now making up over 35% of the S&P 500, up from 12% a decade ago. Hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and others — have poured hundreds of billions into datacentres, increasingly funded by debt, hedge fund positions and retail borrowing. In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF assesses system-wide risks. It now ranks an AI market correction alongside rising government borrowing costs and a major cyber-attack as the three most salient threats to stability, noting that global exposure to US AI assets is the highest it has ever been.
key_points: The IMF names an AI share price correction one of three 'salient risks' to global stability, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a large cyber-attack. It calls the trio 'plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil', meaning a sell-off could quickly spread beyond tech stocks into credit and currency markets.

Market concentration is extreme. The magnificent seven — Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — account for more than 35% of the S&P 500, versus 12% ten years ago, and their combined market value has grown over 50% in two years. The IMF says global exposure to US AI assets is the highest on record.

Leverage is the amplifier. The IMF points to soaring corporate debt, hedge fund bets on the sector and retail investors borrowing to speculate, plus 'circular financing' deals tying strong AI firms to weaker partners. It cites $300bn of hyperscaler deals with weaker AI firms, $650bn of debt and $1.4tn in future commitments in just three years.

The IMF questions the returns. It sees 'growing evidence' that a successful AI rollout 'may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken' by hyperscalers, and that 'potential economic gains may not be as large as expected' — a direct challenge to current capex assumptions.

Exposure is uneven. A correction would hit the US and Asian markets hardest, while the UK and euro area look more insulated — though any investor holding US assets, including pension funds, would still feel the effects through wealth and portfolio losses.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the warning is a signal that cheap capital and unquestioned capex growth may not last: a correction would raise funding costs, force consolidation and push hyperscalers to justify datacentre spending with measurable revenue. For developers, the paradox is that a downturn could help — cheaper compute, open-weight models and a shift from infrastructure hype to applications and efficiency. For regular users, the risk is indirect but real: index funds, pensions and savings are heavily exposed to the same handful of AI stocks, and a sharp repricing could dent household wealth, consumer confidence and the broader economy that currently leans on AI-driven investment.
report.tools: To follow the risk, track the IMF Global Financial Stability Report and BIS/FSB financial-stability notes; use SEC EDGAR full-text search to read hyperscaler debt and capex disclosures directly. For open-source research, OpenBB offers a free investment analytics terminal, and Epoch AI publishes open datasets on compute and AI investment trends. MLCommons benchmarks and Hugging Face leaderboards help gauge whether AI efficiency gains are reducing the need for massive infrastructure spend.
